hints: Think about what ideal means for an amplifier - it should amplify perfectly without affecting the circuit connected to its inputs and without any loss at its output.
Recall the extreme limiting values used in the ideal model for voltage gain, for how much current enters the inputs, and for output resistance.
walkthrough:
**What ideal means**
Think of a perfect voltage amplifier sitting between its inputs and its output. It should respond to even the tiniest input difference with a huge output, it should draw no current from the sensors connected to it, and it should deliver its output voltage without any drop inside itself.

**Pick two defining extremes**
In the ideal model this becomes $$A_{OL} \to \infty$$ for the open-loop gain, and $$R_{IN} \to \infty$$ so that no current flows into the $+$ and $-$ inputs. Equally correct is $$R_{OUT} = 0$$ so the full output voltage appears across the load, or infinite bandwidth and infinite slew rate.
Final answer: Infinite open-loop gain and infinite input impedance (any two from: infinite open-loop gain, infinite input impedance, zero output impedance, infinite bandwidth, infinite slew rate).

hints: Look closely at the symbols - X is a resistor whose resistance changes with its surroundings, and Y is the dashed box where a small coil current closes a separate switch for the lamp.
walkthrough:
**Reading the two symbols**
On the left, X has the resistor box with a diagonal arrow showing its resistance depends on temperature. That is the standard symbol for a thermistor. On the right, the dashed box Y contains a coil that magnetically closes the switch in series with lamp L when energised. That combination is a relay, allowing the tiny op-amp output current to switch the larger lamp current.
Final answer: X is a thermistor (NTC thermistor) and Y is a relay.

hints: Check for a feedback connection between output and the inverting input - there is no resistor feeding the output back, so think about what the very large open-loop gain will do to even a tiny input difference.
Consider the two cases $V^+ > V^-$ and $V^- > V^+$ separately and remember the output cannot exceed the supply rails.
walkthrough:
**No feedback means huge multiplication**
The output is $$V_{OUT} = A_{OL}(V^+ - V^-)$$ with $$A_{OL}$$ enormous for an ideal op-amp. Because there is no feedback path in Fig. 7.1, even a fraction of a millivolt difference at the inputs tries to give thousands of volts at the output.

**Why only two levels**
The output cannot go beyond the power supplies, so it clips or saturates. If $$V^+ > V^-$$ the output is driven hard positive to about the +5 V rail. If $$V^- > V^+$$ it is driven hard negative to about the -5 V rail. Those two saturated states are the only stable outputs.

Final answer: There is no (negative) feedback so the op-amp is open-loop. Any difference between $V^+$ and $V^-$ is multiplied by the very large open-loop gain and drives the output into saturation. It saturates positively near +5 V if $V^+ > V^-$ and negatively near -5 V if $V^- > V^+$.

hints: Think of the name given to an open-loop op-amp circuit whose job is simply to compare the two input voltages and switch high or low.
walkthrough:
**Comparing two voltages**
Here the op-amp is just deciding which input is larger, $V^+$ or $V^-$, and switching its output high or low accordingly. A circuit used in this open-loop switching mode is called a comparator.

hints: Start with the fixed reference - the two identical resistors R form a divider between +5 V and -5 V, so work out the steady voltage at the non-inverting input.
Now follow what happens to the inverting input when temperature rises and the NTC thermistor resistance falls, and link a positive op-amp output through the diode to the relay and lamp.
walkthrough:
**Reference at the + input**
The two resistors R are identical between +5 V and -5 V, so the potential at $V^+$ is midway: $$V^+ = 0\text{ V}$$ This is the fixed level to beat.

**Sensing divider at the - input**
$V^-$ is the junction of variable resistor V and thermistor X between +5 V and -5 V. For an NTC thermistor, higher temperature means lower resistance of X, so more of the 10 V total drops across V and $V^-$ moves down toward -5 V.

**Switching the lamp on**
When it is hot enough that $$V^- < V^+ = 0\text{ V}$$ the comparator saturates positively near +5 V. That forward-biases the diode, current flows in coil Y, the relay closes, and lamp L connects between +5 V and -5 V and lights. So L lights when temperature is above the set threshold.

Final answer: The lamp lights when the temperature is above a particular threshold value. Then $V^- < V^+$, output saturates positive, diode conducts, relay Y is energised and closes the switch for lamp L.

hints: Think about what changing V does to the divider voltage at $V^-$ for a given thermistor resistance, and therefore to the temperature needed to make $V^-$ cross $V^+$.
walkthrough:
**Setting the trip point**
Changing V changes the share of voltage dropped across the sensing divider, so it changes the value of $V^-$ at any given temperature. That means the temperature at which $V^-$ just falls below $V^+$ and the output flips positive can be moved up or down. V is the sensitivity or threshold control.
Final answer: To adjust or set the temperature at which the lamp switches on.
